title: Inquiry told man wanted suicide by cop
article: A Calgary judge said she's "troubled" a one-man police unit was sent to the scene of an armed robbery and hostage taking where an officer was forced to shoot and kill a knife-wielding offender.

A fatality inquiry Tuesday heard that the officer became embroiled in a situation involving a man seeking a lethal dose of drugs and looking to die at the hands of someone else -- a phenomenon known as suicide by cop.
Provincial court Judge Heather Lamoureux said she may put forth a recommendation under Alberta's Fatality Inquiries Act to make it mandatory for officers responding to robberies to be with a partner.
"I want to know from the Calgary police force why we can't have two-person units," Lamoureux said during the hearing into the shooting death of 34-year-old Arthur George Provencal.

Provencal, who was on parole at the time of the incident, was shot between the eyes by Const. Julien Gagne as he held a knife to the throat of an employee during a bungled robbery on Dec. 23, 2000, at Shoppers Drug Mart in TD Square.

Lamoureux said she has no doubt in her mind that Gagne did the right thing by shooting Provencal as he pressed the 30- centimetre blade against Ernie Paxton -- an employee who put himself between the agitated man and three frightened co-workers.
"If that officer (Gagne) . . . had not acted as he did, I dare say Mr. Paxton would have been killed," said Lamoureux.
Calgary police Sgt. Brian Willis, who trains officers on the use of force, said all evidence from the shooting indicates Provencal was looking for someone else to help him take his life.
"When (they) go in looking for suicide . . . they may take action for us to be the vehicle for that," said Willis.

Several other witnesses, who wept openly in court as they listened to the original 911 call to police, testified Tuesday at the inquiry that Provencal walked behind the counter of the downtown store shortly before closing and demanded drugs.
"He said, 'I'm here because you're going to help me die,' " said Yasmin Kanji, the pharmacist on duty at the time.
Paxton told the court Provencal demanded a fatal dose of drugs to "cook up," and two needles.
"He asked for two syringes and said I was going to inject one of them and he'd do the other himself," testified Paxton. "We were stalling. We didn't have the kinds of drugs that he needed."
Another staffer, Sarah Lilly, said Provencal waved around a large meat-cutting knife as he stormed the pharmacy at the back of the building.
"He wanted to die. This was it. He wanted to have the drugs," she testified.
Provencal had been on statutory release from Drumheller Institution where he was serving a federal sentence for armed robbery.

In 1987, he was charged with attempted murder following a knife attack in Ottawa. Those charges were reduced when Provencal, then 21, pleaded guilty to assault and was handed a 20-month jail sentence.

Gagne told the court he arrived on scene just before 6 p.m., to find Provencal behind the counter threatening the staff. He ordered him to drop the knife. Then Provencal reached out and grabbed Paxton, forcing the knife to his throat.

Gagne gave one more warning to drop the weapon before firing off a single shot from his 40-calibre Glock semi-automatic pistol, striking Provencal between the eyes -- the only part of his body that was visible during the brief hostage-taking.
The day-long inquiry heard there were only five on-duty officers in the downtown core when the call came in about the robbery in progress.
"The question is, is there a staffing shortage and is there any recommendation we can make with regards to that?" she said.

The Calgary Police Service has been struggling with staffing levels. A recent police business plan states 32 per cent of officers have completed 25 years of service or will have in the next five years, making them eligible for retirement.
Lamoureux adjourned the fatality inquiry to await several reports from the police service.
